GEN: The book of beginnings: creation, the fall, the flood, and the call of Abraham and the patriarchs. It sets up the covenant promises that run through the whole Bible. Traditionally ascribed to Moses.
EXO: The liberation from Egypt, the Passover, the covenant at Sinai and the Ten Commandments, and the building of the tabernacle.
LEV: Laws of sacrifice, priesthood, ritual purity and holiness ('Be holy, for I am holy'), including the Day of Atonement.
NUM: Israel's wandering in the wilderness after Sinai: censuses, rebellions, and the approach to the promised land.
DEU: Moses' farewell addresses restating the Law and the covenant before Israel enters the land, including the Shema (Deut 6:4).
JOS: The conquest and division of the promised land under Joshua. (Douay-Rheims: Josue.)
JDG: The cycles of sin, oppression and deliverance by judges such as Deborah, Gideon and Samson.
RUT: A short story of loyalty and providence: Ruth the Moabite, who becomes an ancestor of David.
1SA: The prophet Samuel, the anointing of Saul as first king, and the rise of David. (Douay-Rheims: 1 Kings.)
2SA: David's reign over Israel: Jerusalem, the covenant promise of a lasting dynasty, and David's sin and repentance. (Douay-Rheims: 2 Kings.)
1KI: Solomon's reign and the Temple, the division of the kingdom, and the prophet Elijah. (Douay-Rheims: 3 Kings.)
2KI: The history of the divided monarchy through the fall of Samaria and Jerusalem and the exile; the prophet Elisha. (Douay-Rheims: 4 Kings.)
1CH: A retelling of Israel's history from Adam through David, with emphasis on the Temple and worship. (Douay-Rheims: 1 Paralipomenon.)
2CH: The history of Solomon and the kings of Judah to the Babylonian exile and Cyrus's edict. (Douay-Rheims: 2 Paralipomenon.)
EZR: The return from exile and rebuilding of the Temple; Ezra's reform. (Douay-Rheims: 1 Esdras.)
NEH: Nehemiah's rebuilding of the walls of Jerusalem and renewal of the covenant. (Douay-Rheims: 2 Esdras.)
TOB: A deuterocanonical story of a faithful family in exile, the journey of Tobias with the angel Raphael, and the blessings of prayer, almsgiving and marriage. (Douay-Rheims: Tobias.)
JDT: A deuterocanonical story of the widow Judith, who delivers her besieged people through faith and courage. It is a work of religious fiction with a theological purpose rather than strict history.
EST: Esther, a Jewish queen in the Persian court, saves her people. The Catholic canon includes the Greek additions (prayers, the king's edicts and Mordecai's dream), which the Vulgate/Douay numbers as chapters 10:4–16:24.
1MA: A deuterocanonical history of the Maccabean revolt against Antiochus IV and the rededication of the Temple (Hanukkah). (Douay-Rheims: 1 Machabees.)
2MA: A deuterocanonical account of part of the same period, emphasising martyrdom, prayer for the dead and the resurrection hope. (Douay-Rheims: 2 Machabees.)
JOB: The suffering of the righteous Job and his dialogue with friends and with God, addressing the mystery of innocent suffering.
PSA: The 150 prayers of Israel, used in the Church's liturgy and the Liturgy of the Hours. The Vulgate/Douay numbering differs from the Hebrew for Psalms 9–147; the app always shows both.
PRO: Collected wisdom sayings on living well before God, many attributed to Solomon.
ECC: Qoheleth's reflection on the limits of human striving 'under the sun' and the call to fear God. (Douay-Rheims: Ecclesiastes.)
SNG: A love poem read by the Church as an image of God's covenant love and of the soul's union with God. (Douay-Rheims: Canticle of Canticles.)
WIS: A deuterocanonical book of wisdom, written in Greek, on righteousness, immortality and the history of salvation, attributed to Solomon.
SIR: A deuterocanonical book of practical and spiritual wisdom by Jesus ben Sira, in Hebrew c. 180 BC and translated into Greek by his grandson. (Douay-Rheims: Ecclesiasticus.)
ISA: The great prophet of Jerusalem: judgment, consolation and the promise of the Messiah, including the Servant Songs. (Douay-Rheims: Isaias.)
JER: The prophet of the Temple's destruction and of the new covenant (Jer 31).
LAM: Five poems mourning the fall of Jerusalem.
BAR: A deuterocanonical book: Baruch's prayer of repentance, a poem on Wisdom, and the Letter of Jeremiah (ch. 6).
EZK: The prophet-priest in exile: visions of the divine glory, judgment and restoration, the dry bones and the new Temple. (Douay-Rheims: Ezechiel.)
DAN: Court tales and apocalyptic visions of Daniel in exile. The Catholic canon includes the Greek additions: the Prayer of Azariah and Song of the Three (3:24–90), Susanna (ch. 13) and Bel and the Dragon (ch. 14).
HOS: Hosea's marriage as an image of God's faithful love for unfaithful Israel. (Douay-Rheims: Osee.)
JOL: A prophecy of locusts, the Day of the Lord and the outpouring of the Spirit (quoted at Pentecost, Acts 2).
AMO: A shepherd-prophet's call for justice in eighth-century Israel.
OBA: A short oracle against Edom. (Douay-Rheims: Abdias.)
JON: The reluctant prophet sent to Nineveh and God's mercy to repentant sinners. (Douay-Rheims: Jonas.)
MIC: Judgment and hope, including the prophecy of a ruler from Bethlehem (Mic 5). (Douay-Rheims: Micheas.)
NAM: An oracle on the fall of Nineveh.
HAB: A prophet's questions about injustice and the answer 'the just shall live by faith.' (Douay-Rheims: Habacuc.)
ZEP: The Day of the Lord and the remnant of the humble. (Douay-Rheims: Sophonias.)
HAG: A call to rebuild the Temple after the return from exile. (Douay-Rheims: Aggeus.)
ZEC: Visions and oracles of restoration, including the humble king on a donkey (Zech 9). (Douay-Rheims: Zacharias.)
MAL: The last of the prophets: purity of worship and the coming messenger. (Douay-Rheims: Malachias.)
MAT: The Gospel presenting Jesus as the Messiah and new Moses, with five great discourses including the Sermon on the Mount, and the commission to Peter (Mt 16).
MRK: The shortest and probably earliest Gospel: Jesus as the suffering Son of God, moving swiftly to the Passion.
LUK: The Gospel of mercy and of the poor, with the infancy narratives, the parables of the Good Samaritan and Prodigal Son, and the Emmaus road.
JHN: The Gospel of the Word made flesh, with signs and 'I am' sayings, the Bread of Life discourse (ch. 6) and the farewell discourse.
ACT: Luke's account of the Church from the Ascension and Pentecost through Paul's journeys to Rome.
ROM: Paul's most systematic letter: sin, grace, faith and justification, life in the Spirit, Israel and Christian living.
1CO: Paul addresses divisions and disorder at Corinth: the Eucharist (chs. 10–11), the body of Christ, love (ch. 13) and the resurrection (ch. 15).
2CO: Paul's defence of his ministry, the collection for Jerusalem, and strength in weakness.
GAL: Freedom in Christ and justification by faith, against requiring Gentile converts to keep the Mosaic law.
EPH: The Church as the body of Christ, salvation by grace, unity and the Christian household.
PHP: A letter of joy from prison, containing the Christ hymn (Phil 2:6–11).
COL: The supremacy of Christ over all creation and the Church as his body.
1TH: Paul's earliest letter: encouragement, holiness, and hope concerning the return of Christ.
2TH: Further teaching on the Lord's coming and steadfastness.
1TI: A pastoral letter on Church order, worship and sound teaching.
2TI: Paul's final charge to Timothy: fidelity, suffering and the inspiration of Scripture (2 Tim 3:16).
TIT: A pastoral letter on appointing leaders and good works in the Church in Crete.
PHM: A personal appeal to Philemon on behalf of the runaway slave Onesimus.
HEB: Christ as the great High Priest and the fulfilment of the Old Covenant, with a catalogue of the heroes of faith (ch. 11).
JAS: Practical wisdom: faith demonstrated in works, control of the tongue, prayer for the sick (5:14–15).
1PE: Encouragement to Christians facing hostility: the royal priesthood and hope in suffering.
2PE: A warning against false teachers and an assurance of the Lord's return; a statement on the inspiration of prophecy.
1JN: God is light and love; fellowship with God and one another.
2JN: A short letter on truth and love, warning against false teachers.
3JN: A short letter praising hospitality to travelling missionaries.
JUD: A short warning against false teachers, with references to Jewish tradition.
REV: John's apocalyptic vision of the victory of Christ, the heavenly liturgy and the new heavens and new earth. (Douay-Rheims: Apocalypse.)
